card.name: soke
card.tagline: Tongan stick-striking group dance performed in four-person boat formations.
card.profile: The sōkē, also known historically as eke, is a Tongan group dance in which performers rhythmically strike wooden sticks against one another to the beat of a drum. Arranged in four-person units called vaka (boats), two men holding two-meter long sticks pair with two women carrying paired 40-centimeter sticks. The performance serves no secret ceremonial function beyond dazzling audiences and honoring chiefs. Following the 1946 volcanic evacuation of Niuafoʻou, the dance spread across Tonga, evolving into a vibrant public tradition.
card.insight: In 1946, a volcanic eruption on Niuafoʻou displaced its dancers to ʻEua, bringing the stick-striking sōkē dance into mainstream Tonga through the Catholic diocese of Maʻufanga.
card.profile_long:
The origins and history of the sōkē—originally called eke—remain a subject of historical discussion. Anthropologist Harley Harris Bartlett suggested an agricultural root, while historian Edwin Burrows identified a distinctly martial character in its movements. Popular accounts from the tabloid The Catholic Weekly trace its tradition to acts of penance following the 1841 killing of the Catholic priest Peter Chanel on Futuna. Brought alongside early Catholic missionary efforts, the dance moved first to Tafahi and Niuafoʻou. A turning point occurred in 1946 when a devastating volcanic eruption forced the resettlement of Niuafoʻou's population onto ʻEua. From ʻEua, the eke migrated to the Catholic diocese of Maʻufanga on Tongatapu, integrating the stick dance into the Tongan national mainstream.

How the dance is executed centers on spatial coordination and precise stick contact. The basic structural unit is the vaka (boat), comprising two men and two women facing each other. Men typically wield a long stick measuring roughly two meters, whereas women carry two shorter sticks measuring around 40 centimeters each. On the drum cadence, dancers strike sticks in coordinated repeating four-beat sequences. In the first movement, a woman strikes the top of a man's stick with her right stick, hits the bottom with her left, and returns to the top with her right, using the fourth beat to turn and prepare for the next rotation. Alternate patterns involve striking the center of the long stick as a shield, or turning the stick entirely. Formations fall into two structural categories: Eke nou (short eke), where each four-person boat interacts internally, and Eke loa (long eke), where boats exchange dancers across rows on the floor.

Music and instruments provide the essential rhythmic foundation. The dance is driven by a drum pulse alongside recited verses. Dancers remain stationary during spoken stanzas and engage in stick hitting exclusively during refrains, such as the recurring call 'sōkē' or 'hina hea'. The song texts contain archaic vocabulary, incorporating ancient seafaring terms and regional references to figures like King Lavelua of Uvea or geographic landmarks like Pua-toli-nofo on Tafahi. The language of older refrains blends archaic Uvean, Futunan, and Tongan dialects.

In terms of costume and setting, specific traditional attire details are not described in sources. Performance settings historically range from village grounds and church dioceses like Maʻufanga to international gatherings such as the 1972 South Pacific Festival in Suva, Fiji. Occasions and meaning focus on public display and chief honor; as with many Tongan dances, the performance carries no hidden purpose, intended entirely to entertain spectators and show respect to community leaders.

Notable figures associated with the sōkē include historical scholars Edwin Burrows and Harley Harris Bartlett, as well as historic religious figures Pierre Chanel, Pierre Bataillon, Marie Nizier, and King Lavelua of Hahake. Regional variants exist across the Pacific islands, including Uvean eke from Wallis Island, Futunan variations, and regional Tongan adaptations spanning Tafahi, Niuafoʻou, ʻEua, and Tongatapu. In lineage terms, while sharing superficial elements with English Morris dancing, the sōkē represents an entirely independent Pacific development.

sections.origins_and_history: The origins of the eke (sōkē) are disputed. Historian Edwin Burrows noted its martial character, whereas anthropologist Harley Harris Bartlett suggested agricultural roots. The Catholic Weekly reported an origin linked to penance for the 1841 killing of Catholic priest Peter Chanel. Catholic missions brought the eke to Tafahi and Niuafoʻou. Following the 1946 volcanic eruption on Niuafoʻou, residents resettled on ʻEua, after which the dance entered mainstream Tonga via the Catholic diocese of Maʻufanga on Tongatapu.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced in four-person units called vaka ('boat') containing two men and two women facing each other. Men hold long sticks (~2 meters) while women hold two short sticks (~40 cm). Striking occurs on drum beats in four-count phrases: beat 1 top hit, beat 2 bottom hit, beat 3 top hit, beat 4 spatial transition. The dance features two structural modes: Eke nou (short eke, where boats interact only internally) and Eke loa (long eke, where front and back rows exchange performers).
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompanied by drum beat and vocal chanting. Performers stand still during recited stanzas and strike sticks during refrains (such as 'sōkē' or 'hina hea'). Lyrics incorporate archaic Uvean, Futunan, and Tongan words along with historical seafaring terms.
sections.costume_and_setting: Specific attire details are not described in sources. Performance settings include community venues, the Catholic diocese of Maʻufanga on Tongatapu, and international regional events like the 1972 South Pacific Festival in Suva.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed to dazzle spectators and please community chiefs. The dance has no hidden ritual purpose.
sections.notable_figures: Historian Edwin Burrows, anthropologist Harley Harris Bartlett, Saint Peter Chanel, Father Pierre Bataillon, Marie Nizier, and King Lavelua.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the Uvean eke from Wallis Island (performed in Suva in 1972), Futunan eke, and Tongan regional versions from Tafahi, Niuafoʻou, ʻEua, and Maʻufanga.
sections.lineage: Developed independently in the Pacific, though sharing structural stick-striking features with English Morris dance.

basic_steps: Form a four-person vaka with two men facing two women.
Stand stationary during the recited vocal stanzas.
On count 1 of refrain, women strike right stick to the top of the man's long stick.
On count 2, women strike left stick to the bottom of the man's long stick.
On count 3, women strike right stick back to the top of the man's long stick.
On count 4, execute a quarter turn to transition to the next stick interaction.
teaching.rhythm: Four-beat pulse aligned with drum rhythm
teaching.formation: Four-person rectangular units (vaka) arranged in lines
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on four-beat timing and stick alignment in Eke nou before attempting row exchanges in Eke loa.

claims.text: Sōkē or eke is a Tongan group dance performed with sticks which the performers hit against each other on the beat of the drum.
As with most Tongan dances, the whole performance is to dazzle the spectators and to please the chiefs.
The Catholic Weekly claimed origin as penance for the 1841 killing of Peter Chanel.
The 1946 volcanic eruption on Niuafoʻou caused resettlement of its people to ʻEua.
A single boat unit consists of two men and two women facing each other.
Men carry one long stick of about 2 meters while women carry short sticks of about 40 cm in each hand.
In Eke nou, individual four-person boats interact only with themselves.
In Eke loa, boats exchange dancers between rows.
The dance is currently better known in Tonga by the refrain sōkē.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Steady drum beat driving 4-count stick-striking refrains alternated with un-struck vocal verses.
music_profile.vocal_style: Group chant and recited stanzas alternating with refrain songs.
music_profile.musical_form: Stanza recitation (stationary) alternating with refrain (stick striking).
music_profile.sound_description: Percussive rhythmic beating of wooden sticks striking together and hitting the ground over a driving drum pulse, punctuated by vocal group refrain chants.

movement_profile.posture: Upright facing partner in four-person vaka unit.
movement_profile.footwork: Transitions and turns performed on the 4th beat of each stick-striking phrase.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Men hold one 2-meter long stick; women hold two 40-cm short sticks.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Controlled torso orientation facing partners or shifting diagonally.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Vaka (boat) units of 4 dancers in rows; Eke nou stays within unit, Eke loa exchanges rows.
movement_profile.partnering: Paired stick contact between men and women facing or positioned diagonally.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Rhythmic and punctuated on every drum beat.

signature_moves.description: Short stick dance where each four-person vaka interacts strictly within its own group.

signature_moves.name: Eke loa
signature_moves.description: Long stick dance where four-person boats exchange row positions across the floor.

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid misaligned stick strikes to ensure safety during rapid four-beat contact patterns.

episode_brief.title_hook: Rhythms of the Vaka: The Tongan Sōkē
episode_brief.logline: Explore how a displaced island community preserved and popularized the vibrant stick-striking sōkē dance across Tonga.
beats: Introduce the island of Niuafoʻou and the 1946 eruption that relocated its dancers to ʻEua.
Demonstrate the vaka formation of four dancers holding short and long wooden sticks.
Break down the fundamental four-beat stick striking cadence against the drum beat.
Contrast the self-contained Eke nou with the row-exchanging Eke loa.
Show a full group performance featuring the chorus refrain 'sōkē'.

drills: Practice top-bottom-top stick hits on counts 1-2-3.
Practice turning on count 4 to reset position.
Perform diagonal stick strikes across the vaka.
Coordinate male shield holds with female double-stick hits.
Execute front-to-back row shifts on beat 4 during continuous chanting.

seniors.seated_version: Performers sit in facing pairs, using shortened sticks to tap counts 1-3 on partner's stick and resting on count 4.
seniors.standing_version: Perform stationary stick contact without row-exchanging movements.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduce tempo to comfortable pace; restrict stick reach to shoulder height.
seniors.counts: Counts 1-2-3 for soft stick contact, count 4 for pause.

children.game_version: Play 'Boat Captain' where four-child vaka teams try to complete 4 consecutive striking rounds without dropping rhythm.
avoid: Heavy wooden sticks (use foam or light bamboo dowels)
